text.hg: Police in Rajasthan's Alwar district caught more than 60 sextortion gangs in the year to September 2021, and 13 of those caught were minors aged 14 to 16, Dainik Bhaskar reported; a senior Maharashtra Cyber police officer wrote in March 2022 that such rackets operate from towns such as Mewat, Bharatpur and Alwar in Rajasthan and Haryana.

facts.caveat: Figures come from local police via news reports, not official statistics. The usual method is a video call from a fake profile posing as a woman; the call is recorded and used for blackmail, sometimes followed by calls from people posing as police.

text.en: A senior Maharashtra Cyber police officer estimated in March 2022 that India sees more than 500 sextortion cases a day; WeProtect Global Alliance repeated the figure in a June 2024 briefing.
text.hg: A senior Maharashtra Cyber police officer estimated in March 2022 that India sees more than 500 sextortion cases a day; WeProtect Global Alliance repeated the figure in a June 2024 briefing.

facts.caveat: An official's estimate, not measured data; present it only as an estimate, never as a statistic.

text.en: Reports of financially motivated sextortion to NCMEC's CyberTipline rose from more than 10,000 in 2022 to more than 28,000 in 2023, according to NCMEC's year-by-year data.
text.hg: Reports of financially motivated sextortion to NCMEC's CyberTipline rose from more than 10,000 in 2022 to more than 28,000 in 2023, according to NCMEC's year-by-year data.

facts.caveat: WeProtect's June 2024 brief gave 10,731 (2022) and 26,718 (2023) from earlier NCMEC data; NCMEC's later chart shows more than 28,000 for 2023. NCMEC reported more than 36,000 in 2024 and more than 50,000 in 2025 (see dig-ncmec-financial-sextortion-2025). Global reports, not India-specific.

text.en: Financial sexual extortion mainly targets teenage boys aged 13 to 17, who are typically deceived into believing they are talking to a young woman; the move from first message to coercion can take minutes to hours, and 70% of victims who ignore payment demands do not have their images distributed, according to WeProtect.
text.hg: WeProtect ke mutabik, financial sexual extortion ka main nishana 13 se 17 saal ke teenage ladke hote hain, jinhein aam taur par dhokhe se yeh yakeen dilaya jaata hai ki woh kisi young woman se baat kar rahe hain. Pehle message se coercion (zabardasti) tak pahunchne mein kuch minute se lekar kuch ghante lag sakte hain, aur payment ki maang ko ignore karne wale 70% victims ki tasveerein failayi nahin jaatin.

facts.value: boys 13-17; 70% not distributed after ignoring demands
facts.caveat: Global evidence summary; the 70% figure comes from a cited study, not Indian data.

text.en: In a 2023 Snap survey of more than 6,000 teens and young adults in six countries including India, 65% said they or their friends had been targeted in online sextortion schemes through catfishing or hacking.
text.hg: 2023 mein Snap ke ek survey mein India samet chhah deshon ke 6,000 se zyada teens aur young adults mein se 65% ne kaha ki unhein ya unke doston ko catfishing (fake pehchaan se dhokha) ya hacking ke zariye online sextortion schemes ka nishana banaya gaya tha.

facts.caveat: Pooled six-country result commissioned by a platform; India-specific figure not given here. 'They or their friends' inflates prevalence.

text.en: In August 2026 I4C warned that fake pornography apps advertised on Facebook and Instagram under names such as 'Night Play', 'Reloop' and 'Kyss' were being used to take over Android phones and commit financial fraud.
text.hg: August 2026 mein I4C ne warning di ki Facebook aur Instagram par 'Night Play', 'Reloop' aur 'Kyss' jaise naamon se advertise kiye gaye fake pornography apps ka istemaal Android phones par kabza karne aur financial fraud karne ke liye kiya ja raha tha.

text.en: Since 2021, India's Digital Media Ethics Code has required streaming platforms to provide parental locks for content rated U/A 13+ or higher and a 'reliable age verification mechanism' for adult ('A') content.
text.hg: 2021 se India ke Digital Media Ethics Code ke tahat streaming platforms ke liye U/A 13+ ya usse upar ki rating wale content par parental lock, aur adult ('A') content ke liye 'reliable age verification mechanism' dena zaroori hai.

facts.caveat: Applies to publishers of online curated content (OTT services); the IT Rules text reviewed contains no comparable age-check duty for other websites hosting adult content, and enforcement of the OTT age check is not documented.

text.en: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 defines a child as anyone under 18 and requires platforms to obtain verifiable parental consent before processing a child's personal data, and bars tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising aimed at children.
text.hg: India ka Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 har us vyakti ko 'child' (bachcha) define karta hai jiski umr 18 saal se kam hai. Yeh platforms ke liye kisi bachche ka personal data process karne se pehle verifiable parental consent lena zaroori banata hai, aur bachchon ko nishana banakar ki jaane wali tracking, behavioural monitoring aur targeted advertising par rok lagata hai.

facts.caveat: Section 1(2) lets the government bring provisions into force on different dates; when Section 9 takes effect, and the age-verification method under the DPDP Rules, 2025, were not verified in this check, so do not describe these duties as already enforced without checking.

text.en: India's National Crime Records Bureau signed a memorandum of understanding with the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children on 26 April 2019 to receive CyberTipline reports on online child sexual abuse material and child sexual exploitation, the government told the Rajya Sabha in July 2024.
text.hg: India's National Crime Records Bureau signed a memorandum of understanding with the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children on 26 April 2019 to receive CyberTipline reports on online child sexual abuse material and child sexual exploitation, the government told the Rajya Sabha in July 2024.

facts.caveat: This is how NCMEC tips reach Indian police; by 31 March 2024 more than 69.05 lakh such reports had been shared with states.

text.en: The government has disabled public access in India to 50 OTT streaming platforms in two years for showing obscene content, citing Sections 67 and 67A of the IT Act, Section 294 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Indecent Representation of Women Act, the Information and Broadcasting Ministry told the Lok Sabha on 22 July 2026; the count stood at 43 in December 2025.
text.hg: The government has disabled public access in India to 50 OTT streaming platforms in two years for showing obscene content, citing Sections 67 and 67A of the IT Act, Section 294 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Indecent Representation of Women Act, the Information and Broadcasting Ministry told the Lok Sabha on 22 July 2026; the count stood at 43 in December 2025.

facts.caveat: Blocked services have reappeared on new domains (see dig-ott-block-2026).

text.en: India sent the second-largest number of visitors, after the United States, to NCMEC's Take It Down image-removal site in 2025, when the site recorded more than 1.6 million visitors; by the end of 2025 the service was available in 36 languages.
text.hg: India sent the second-largest number of visitors, after the United States, to NCMEC's Take It Down image-removal site in 2025, when the site recorded more than 1.6 million visitors; by the end of 2025 the service was available in 36 languages.

facts.value: India 2nd by visitors; 1.6 million visitors; 36 languages
facts.caveat: Visitor counts show demand, not the number of images removed.

text.en: Since 2021 India's IT Rules have required large social media platforms to use automated tools to proactively identify content depicting rape or child sexual abuse, and copies of content already taken down; the February 2026 amendment turned the duty to 'endeavour to deploy' such tools into a duty to 'deploy appropriate technical measures'.
text.hg: Since 2021 India's IT Rules have required large social media platforms to use automated tools to proactively identify content depicting rape or child sexual abuse, and copies of content already taken down; the February 2026 amendment turned the duty to 'endeavour to deploy' such tools into a duty to 'deploy appropriate technical measures'.

facts.caveat: Applies to significant social media intermediaries; the rule requires measures to be proportionate to free speech and privacy interests.

text.en: When the relationship to the victim was known, 94% of sextortion reports made to NCMEC by the public came from the child victim or a parent, most of them from children themselves, NCMEC reported in June 2026.
text.hg: When the relationship to the victim was known, 94% of sextortion reports made to NCMEC by the public came from the child victim or a parent, most of them from children themselves, NCMEC reported in June 2026.

facts.caveat: Covers public reports only; most sextortion reports to NCMEC come from platforms. Global, not India-specific.

text.en: An estimated 25.61 lakh (2.56 million) people were living with HIV in India in 2024, the second-largest HIV-positive population in the world after South Africa.
text.hg: 2024 mein India mein andaazan 25.61 lakh (2.56 million) log HIV ke saath jee rahe the; South Africa ke baad yeh duniya mein HIV-positive logon ki doosri sabse badi aabadi thi.

facts.caveat: Modelled estimate from the India HIV Estimates 2025 round (data year 2024), not a count of diagnosed people; each estimation round revises the whole back-series, so do not compare with figures published in older rounds.

text.en: Adult (15-49) HIV prevalence in India was estimated at 0.20% in 2024, against a global average of 0.70%.
text.hg: 2024 mein India mein adults (15-49 saal) mein HIV prevalence andaazan 0.20% thi, jabki global average 0.70% tha.

facts.caveat: A low national average hides concentrated epidemics in the North-East and among key populations.

text.en: India's adult HIV prevalence peaked at around 0.58-0.59% in 1997-98 and fell to about 0.44% in 2005, 0.33% in 2010, 0.27% in 2015, 0.23% in 2020 and 0.20% in 2024.
text.hg: India mein adults ki HIV prevalence 1997-98 mein lagbhag 0.58-0.59% ke peak par thi; iske baad yeh ghat kar 2005 mein lagbhag 0.44%, 2010 mein 0.33%, 2015 mein 0.27%, 2020 mein 0.23% aur 2024 mein 0.20% reh gayi.

facts.caveat: Back-calculated series from the 2025 estimation round. The previous round (Sankalak 2024) gave slightly different values (peak 0.59-0.60%, 0.32% in 2010, 0.22% in 2020), so do not mix figures from different rounds.

text.en: An estimated 64,470 people in India were newly infected with HIV in 2024, a 48.7% fall from about 1.25 lakh new infections in 2010.
text.hg: 2024 mein India mein andaazan 64,470 logon ko naya HIV infection hua, jo 2010 ke lagbhag 1.25 lakh naye infections se 48.7% kam hai.

facts.caveat: The 2010 baseline of 1.25 lakh is from the PIB backgrounder (30 Nov 2025), which rounds 2024 to 64,500. Uncertainty range is wide. NACP-V's own goal was an 80% cut from 2010 by 2025-26, so the 49% fall is well short of target.

text.en: An estimated 32,160 people died of AIDS-related causes in India in 2024, down 81.4% from about 1.73 lakh deaths in 2010.
text.hg: 2024 mein India mein andaazan 32,160 logon ki maut AIDS se jude kaaranon se hui, jo 2010 ki lagbhag 1.73 lakh mauton se 81.4% kam hai.

facts.caveat: Modelled estimate. The 1.73 lakh 2010 baseline is from the PIB backgrounder of 30 Nov 2025 (which rounds 2024 to 32,200).

text.en: India's HIV incidence was 0.05 new infections per 1,000 uninfected people in 2024, but NACO's incidence-mortality ratio stood at 1.07, above the threshold of 1, meaning the number of people living with HIV in India is still slowly growing.
text.hg: 2024 mein India mein HIV incidence har 1,000 uninfected logon par 0.05 naye infections thi, lekin NACO ka incidence-mortality ratio 1.07 tha, jo 1 ki threshold se upar hai. Iska matlab hai ki India mein HIV ke saath jee rahe logon ki sankhya ab bhi dheere-dheere badh rahi hai.

facts.caveat: The incidence-mortality ratio compares new infections with deaths among people living with HIV; NACO says India must intensify prevention to bring it below 1, the marker of a shrinking epidemic.

text.en: In March 2025, 18.60 lakh people living with HIV in India were on antiretroviral therapy: 17.54 lakh at 800 government ART centres and an estimated 1.06 lakh in the private sector.
text.hg: March 2025 mein India mein HIV ke saath jee rahe 18.60 lakh log antiretroviral therapy (ART) le rahe the: 17.54 lakh log 800 sarkari ART centres par aur andaazan 1.06 lakh private sector mein.

facts.caveat: 18.60 lakh of 25.61 lakh estimated PLHIV is about 73% of all PLHIV; ART is free at government centres.

text.en: In 2024-25, 83.9% of people living with HIV in India knew their status, 86.6% of those diagnosed were on treatment and 97.6% of those on treatment were virally suppressed, short of the UN 95-95-95 targets for the first two steps.
text.hg: 2024-25 mein India mein HIV ke saath jee rahe 83.9% logon ko apna HIV status pata tha, jinka diagnosis ho chuka tha unmein se 86.6% treatment par the, aur treatment le rahe logon mein se 97.6% virally suppressed the. Pehle do steps mein yeh UN ke 95-95-95 targets se kam hai.

facts.caveat: Viral suppression percentage is among those tested on treatment; roughly 1 in 6 people with HIV did not know their status in 2024-25.

text.en: HIV prevalence in India in 2024 was 8.79% among people who inject drugs, 2.84% among hijra/transgender people, 2.12% among men who have sex with men and 1.13% among female sex workers, against 0.20% among all adults.
text.hg: 2024 mein India mein HIV prevalence injection se drugs lene wale logon mein 8.79%, hijra/transgender logon mein 2.84%, purushon ke saath sex karne wale purushon mein 2.12% aur female sex workers mein 1.13% thi, jabki sabhi adults mein yeh 0.20% thi.

facts.value: PWID 8.79%; H/TG 2.84%; MSM 2.12%; FSW 1.13%; prison inmates 1.99% (2023); truckers 0.81%; migrants 0.45%
facts.caveat: Sentinel/estimation figures for groups reached by the programme; hidden populations may differ.

text.en: Among 1,63,306 people newly diagnosed with HIV in India in 2024-25 (valid records in NACO's monitoring system), nearly 74% reported heterosexual sex (32.1% with casual partners, 26.5% with regular partners and 15.1% with commercial partners), 11.5% shared needles or syringes, 5.4% homosexual or bisexual sex and 3.5% mother-to-child transmission; 4.7% gave no route.
text.hg: Among 1,63,306 people newly diagnosed with HIV in India in 2024-25 (valid records in NACO's monitoring system), nearly 74% reported heterosexual sex (32.1% with casual partners, 26.5% with regular partners and 15.1% with commercial partners), 11.5% shared needles or syringes, 5.4% homosexual or bisexual sex and 3.5% mother-to-child transmission; 4.7% gave no route.

facts.value: Heterosexual 73.7% (casual 32.1%, regular 26.5%, commercial 15.1%); injecting drug use 11.5%; homosexual/bisexual 5.4%; parent-to-child 3.5%; blood 1.2%; unknown 4.7% (2024-25)
facts.caveat: Self-reported route at diagnosis; stigma pushes under-reporting of sex between men and of drug use.

text.en: The share of newly diagnosed HIV cases in India linked to shared needles and syringes rose from under 3% in 2017-18 to 12.5% in 2023-24 and 11.5% in 2024-25.
text.hg: The share of newly diagnosed HIV cases in India linked to shared needles and syringes rose from under 3% in 2017-18 to 12.5% in 2023-24 and 11.5% in 2024-25.

facts.caveat: Self-reported route at diagnosis. The under-3% figure for 2017-18 comes from NACO's narrative text only. The report's narrative wrongly labels 11.5% as the 2023-24 value; its own figure and table put 11.5% in 2024-25 and 12.5% in 2023-24.

text.en: Mizoram had India's highest adult HIV prevalence in 2024 at 2.75%, nearly 14 times the national average of 0.20%, followed by Nagaland (1.37%) and Manipur (0.81%).
text.hg: 2024 mein adults mein HIV prevalence desh mein sabse zyada Mizoram mein thi, 2.75%, jo 0.20% ke national average ka lagbhag 14 guna hai; iske baad Nagaland (1.37%) aur Manipur (0.81%) the.

facts.caveat: Mizoram's incidence (0.90 per 1,000 uninfected people) is 18 times the national 0.05, signalling active transmission. Among people newly diagnosed in Mizoram in 2024-25, about two-thirds reported heterosexual sex and about a quarter (24%) shared needles (Sankalak Table 2.3).

text.en: Maharashtra had the largest estimated number of people living with HIV in 2024 (3,99,023), followed by Andhra Pradesh (3,10,451), Karnataka (2,91,348), Uttar Pradesh (1,95,427) and Tamil Nadu (1,65,971).
text.hg: Maharashtra had the largest estimated number of people living with HIV in 2024 (3,99,023), followed by Andhra Pradesh (3,10,451), Karnataka (2,91,348), Uttar Pradesh (1,95,427) and Tamil Nadu (1,65,971).

facts.value: Maharashtra 3,99,023; Andhra Pradesh 3,10,451; Karnataka 2,91,348; Uttar Pradesh 1,95,427; Tamil Nadu 1,65,971; Telangana 1,56,961; Bihar 1,54,296
facts.caveat: Modelled estimates. Large southern and western states have high absolute numbers but relatively low incidence; Uttar Pradesh's large count reflects population size (adult prevalence 0.10%).

text.en: The estimated rate of mother-to-child HIV transmission in India fell to 10.25% in 2024-25 from more than 25% in 2020-21, meaning roughly 1 in 10 babies born to mothers with HIV still acquire the virus.
text.hg: India mein maa se bachche mein HIV transmission ki andaazit dar 2020-21 mein 25% se zyada thi, jo 2024-25 mein ghat kar 10.25% reh gayi. Iska matlab hai ki HIV wali maaon se paida hue lagbhag 10 mein se 1 bachche ko ab bhi yeh virus ho jaata hai.

facts.caveat: Modelled rate with a wide uncertainty bound (6.74-16.77%). WHO's elimination benchmark (a transmission rate below 5% in breastfeeding populations) is not stated in this source.

text.en: As of March 2025, eight years after the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act 2017 was passed, 29 States/UTs had notified rules under it, 34 had an Ombudsman and 33 had designated Complaints Officers.
text.hg: HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act 2017 paas hone ke aath saal baad, March 2025 tak 29 States/UTs ne iske tahat rules notify kiye the, 34 mein Ombudsman tha aur 33 ne Complaints Officers designate kiye the.

facts.value: 29 States/UTs with rules; 34 with Ombudsman; 33 with Complaints Officers
facts.caveat: Existence of an Ombudsman does not show how many complaints were filed or resolved.

text.en: NACO runs 1,127 Designated STI/RTI Clinics, branded Suraksha Clinics, at district hospitals and medical colleges across India; Uttar Pradesh has the most (115).
text.hg: NACO poore India ke district hospitals aur medical colleges mein 1,127 Designated STI/RTI Clinics chalata hai, jinhe 'Suraksha Clinic' ka naam diya gaya hai; sabse zyada (115) Uttar Pradesh mein hain.

facts.caveat: Below district level, STI care is delivered by the general health system (CHCs, PHCs, sub-centres); STIs treated by private doctors and quacks are not counted.

text.en: India's AIDS programme managed about 1.12 crore (111.8 lakh) STI/RTI cases in 2024-25, including 71.95 lakh visits at Suraksha Clinics, of which 60.9% were by women.
text.hg: 2024-25 mein India ke AIDS programme ne STI/RTI ke lagbhag 1.12 crore (111.8 lakh) cases manage kiye, jinmein Suraksha Clinics par hui 71.95 lakh visits shaamil hain; inmein se 60.9% visits mahilaon ki thi.

facts.value: 111.8 lakh STI/RTI clients; 71.95 lakh DSRC visits (60.9% female)
facts.caveat: Counts episodes/visits, not unique people; managed largely by syndromic approach (symptoms), so many asymptomatic infections are missed.

text.en: Of 46.2 lakh syphilis screenings at India's government STI clinics in 2024-25, 43,482 (0.94%) were reactive, rising to 1.54% among men and 4.12% among transgender clients, against 0.48% among women.
text.hg: 2024-25 mein India ke sarkari STI clinics mein syphilis ki 46.2 lakh screenings mein se 43,482 (0.94%) reactive nikli; mardon mein yeh dar badh kar 1.54% aur transgender clients mein 4.12% thi, jabki mahilaon mein 0.48%.

facts.caveat: Clinic attendees are a high-risk, self-selected group, not the general population. NACO's executive summary gives 0.60% (2021-22) and 0.70% (2022-23) for earlier years, but its year labels are inconsistent.

text.en: Syphilis positivity among STI clinic attendees in 2024-25 was 14% in Arunachal Pradesh, 11% in Sikkim, 7% in Meghalaya and 4% in Mizoram, against a national average of 0.9%.
text.hg: 2024-25 mein STI clinics aane walon mein syphilis positivity Arunachal Pradesh mein 14%, Sikkim mein 11%, Meghalaya mein 7% aur Mizoram mein 4% thi, jabki national average 0.9% tha.

facts.value: Arunachal Pradesh 14%; Sikkim 11%; Meghalaya 7%; Mizoram 4%; India 0.9%
facts.caveat: Clinic-based positivity, not population prevalence.

text.en: Only 77% of pregnant women in India were tested for syphilis in 2024-25 (up from 30% in 2017-18), compared with 84% tested for HIV.
text.hg: 2024-25 mein India mein sirf 77% pregnant mahilaon ka syphilis test hua (2017-18 ke 30% se badh kar), jabki HIV test 84% ka hua.

facts.caveat: Coverage is against estimated pregnancies; NACO says 2024-25 coverage dipped slightly from 2023-24 due to reporting and supply problems. Roughly 1 in 4 pregnant women were still not tested.

text.en: India identified 10,545 syphilis-infected pregnant women in 2024-25, double the 5,228 found in 2021-22, and 86% of them (9,065) received treatment.
text.hg: 2024-25 mein India mein syphilis se infected 10,545 pregnant mahilaon ki pehchaan hui; yeh sankhya 2021-22 mein mili 5,228 mahilaon ka double hai, aur inmein se 86% (9,065) ko ilaaj mila.

facts.caveat: The rise largely reflects more testing, not necessarily more infection. About 1,480 identified women were not recorded as treated; one dose of benzathine penicillin can prevent congenital syphilis.

text.en: Syphilis positivity among pregnant and breastfeeding women in 2024-25 was 1.86% in Arunachal Pradesh, 1.32% in Meghalaya and 1.15% in Mizoram, against a national average of 0.05%.
text.hg: 2024-25 mein pregnant aur breastfeeding mahilaon mein syphilis positivity Arunachal Pradesh mein 1.86%, Meghalaya mein 1.32% aur Mizoram mein 1.15% thi, jabki national average 0.05% tha.

facts.caveat: The report itself describes Arunachal's rate as 'over eighteen times the national average', which does not match 0.05% (it would be about 37 times); avoid printing a multiple.

text.en: Annual new HIV infections were higher in 2024 than in 2010 in Arunachal Pradesh (up 456%), Tripura (up 447%), Meghalaya (up 59%) and Punjab (up 29%), even as they fell by about half nationally.
text.hg: Arunachal Pradesh (456% upar), Tripura (447% upar), Meghalaya (59% upar) aur Punjab (29% upar) mein 2024 mein saalana naye HIV infections 2010 se zyada the, jabki desh bhar mein yeh lagbhag aadhe reh gaye.

facts.caveat: Negative 'decline' values in NACO's state table mean an increase. Percentage rises in small north-eastern states start from small bases (Tripura: 1,171 new infections in 2024; Arunachal: 328). Assam (+8%) and Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu (+79%) also rose. NACO's narrative says new infections in Punjab and Meghalaya 'nearly doubled', which conflicts with its own table and Figure 2.15 (+29% and +59%); use the table values.

text.en: Bihar recorded India's highest estimated number of new HIV infections in 2024 (7,694), followed by Punjab (6,785), Uttar Pradesh (6,373), Maharashtra (5,334) and Karnataka (4,618).
text.hg: 2024 mein desh mein sabse zyada andaazit naye HIV infections Bihar mein darj hue (7,694), iske baad Punjab (6,785), Uttar Pradesh (6,373), Maharashtra (5,334) aur Karnataka (4,618) rahe.

facts.value: Bihar 7,694; Punjab 6,785; Uttar Pradesh 6,373; Maharashtra 5,334; Karnataka 4,618
facts.caveat: Modelled point estimates with wide uncertainty ranges (Bihar 4,607-12,982). Low-prevalence, high-population states now drive a large share of new infections.

text.en: Only 212 babies were recorded with congenital syphilis in India in 2024-25, of whom 189 (89%) were treated, a tiny number compared with the 10,545 syphilis-infected pregnant women identified that year.
text.hg: 2024-25 mein India mein congenital syphilis wale sirf 212 babies record hue, jinmein se 189 (89%) ka ilaaj hua; usi saal pehchaani gayi syphilis se infected 10,545 pregnant mahilaon ke muqable yeh bahut chhoti sankhya hai.

facts.caveat: Diagnosis relies on clinical examination and follow-up of exposed babies, so the figure is likely an undercount; NACO notes Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Haryana and Chandigarh reported zero treatment despite documented cases.

text.en: The HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 (Act No. 16 of 2017) was enacted in April 2017 but came into force only on 10 September 2018, about 17 months later.
text.hg: HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 (Act No. 16 of 2017) April 2017 mein bana, lekin laagu hua lagbhag 17 mahine baad, 10 September 2018 ko.

facts.value: Act No. 16 of 2017, dated 20 April 2017; in force 10 September 2018
facts.caveat: Act No. 16 of 2017 received assent on 20 April 2017 and was published in the Gazette on 21 April 2017 (Gazette copy hosted by NACO). Section 1(3) made commencement depend on a government notification, which came 16-17 months later.

text.en: Section 3 of India's HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 bars discrimination against people living with HIV, and those who live with them, in employment, healthcare, education, housing, public or private office, insurance (unless based on actuarial studies), and forbids their isolation or segregation and HIV testing as a pre-condition for jobs, healthcare or education.
text.hg: India ke HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 ka Section 3 HIV ke saath jee rahe logon aur unke saath rehne walon ke khilaaf employment, healthcare, education, housing, public ya private office aur insurance (jab tak woh actuarial studies par based na ho) mein discrimination par rok lagata hai; saath hi unhe isolate ya segregate karne, aur jobs, healthcare ya education ke liye HIV test ko pre-condition banane par bhi rok lagata hai.

facts.caveat: 'Protected person' (Section 2(s)) covers people with HIV and people who ordinarily live, or have lived, with someone with HIV. Clause (j) allows insurance differences only if 'supported by actuarial studies'.

text.en: Under Sections 4 and 37 of the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017, anyone who publishes, propagates or advocates hatred against people living with HIV can be punished with imprisonment of three months to two years, a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh, or both.
text.hg: Under Sections 4 and 37 of the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017, anyone who publishes, propagates or advocates hatred against people living with HIV can be punished with imprisonment of three months to two years, a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh, or both.

facts.value: 3 months to 2 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs 1,00,000 (Section 37)
facts.caveat: Section 37 penalises contravention of Section 4 (words, signs or other communication propagating hatred against protected persons). No national data on prosecutions was found.

text.en: India's HIV Act, 2017 forbids HIV testing without informed consent (Section 5), says no one can be compelled to disclose their HIV status except by court order (Section 8), and lets courts hide a person's identity behind a pseudonym in HIV-related cases (Section 34).
text.hg: India ka HIV Act, 2017 informed consent ke bina HIV test par rok lagata hai (Section 5), kehta hai ki court order ke bina kisi ko bhi apna HIV status batane ke liye majboor nahi kiya ja sakta (Section 8), aur courts ko HIV se jude cases mein kisi insaan ki pehchaan ek pseudonym (badle hue naam) ke peeche chhupane ki ijaazat deta hai (Section 34).

facts.caveat: Section 39 fines anyone who discloses a protected person's HIV status learnt through court proceedings up to Rs 1 lakh, unless a court ordered the disclosure.

text.en: Every Indian state must appoint an HIV Ombudsman under the 2017 Act, and anyone who ignores an Ombudsman's order can be fined up to Rs 10,000 plus up to Rs 5,000 for every day the failure continues.
text.hg: 2017 ke Act ke tahat India ke har state ko ek HIV Ombudsman appoint karna zaroori hai, aur Ombudsman ke order ko ignore karne wale par Rs 10,000 tak ka jurmana lag sakta hai, saath hi jitne din order ka paalan na ho, har din ke liye Rs 5,000 tak aur.

facts.value: Fine up to Rs 10,000 + Rs 5,000 per day (Section 38)
facts.caveat: As of March 2025, 34 States/UTs had Ombudsmen (Sankalak 2025; PIB, 30 Nov 2025). Section 28 requires each Ombudsman to report the number and nature of complaints every six months and publish the report online, but no national compilation of complaints or outcomes was found.

text.en: The HIV Act, 2017 obliges central and state governments to provide HIV diagnostics, antiretroviral therapy and treatment of opportunistic infections only 'as far as possible' (Section 14).
text.hg: HIV Act, 2017 central aur state governments par HIV diagnostics, antiretroviral therapy aur opportunistic infections ka ilaaj dene ki zimmedari sirf 'as far as possible' (jahan tak sambhav ho) ki shart ke saath daalta hai (Section 14).

facts.caveat: The qualifier means the Act does not create an absolute legal right to free treatment; in practice ART is free at government centres.

text.en: GLOBOCAN 2022 estimated 1,27,526 new cervical cancer cases and 79,906 cervical cancer deaths in India in 2022, making it the second most common cancer among Indian women (17.7% of their cancers).
text.hg: GLOBOCAN 2022 ke andaaze ke mutabik 2022 mein India mein cervical cancer ke 1,27,526 naye cases aaye aur isse 79,906 mautein hui; is tarah yeh Indian mahilaon mein doosra sabse common cancer tha (unke kul cancer cases ka 17.7%).

facts.value: 127,526 new cases; 79,906 deaths; 9.0% of all new cancers; ASR 17.7 per 100,000 women
facts.caveat: Modelled from 20 sub-national cancer registries; India had no national mortality data ('No data'), so deaths are modelled. The Government of India (PIB, 28 Feb 2026) cites this edition as 'over 1 lakh 20 thousand new cases and nearly 80 thousand deaths'. Superseded by GLOBOCAN 2024 (see sh-cervical-cancer-globocan-2024).

text.en: GLOBOCAN 2022 estimated 1,92,020 new breast cancer cases and 98,337 breast cancer deaths in India in 2022, the most common cancer in the country and 26.6% of all cancers in women.
text.hg: GLOBOCAN 2022 ke andaaze ke mutabik 2022 mein India mein breast cancer ke 1,92,020 naye cases aaye aur isse 98,337 mautein hui; yeh desh ka sabse common cancer tha aur mahilaon ke sabhi cancer cases ka 26.6%.

facts.value: 192,020 new cases; 98,337 deaths; 13.6% of all new cancers
facts.caveat: Modelled estimate; India total in 2022 was 14,13,316 new cancer cases and 9,16,827 cancer deaths.

text.en: India accounted for about 19% of the world's new cervical cancer cases (1,27,526 of 6,62,301) and about 23% of cervical cancer deaths (79,906 of 3,48,874) in 2022.
text.hg: 2022 mein duniya bhar ke cervical cancer ke naye cases mein se lagbhag 19% (6,62,301 mein se 1,27,526) aur isse hui mauton mein se lagbhag 23% (3,48,874 mein se 79,906) India mein the.

facts.caveat: Shares are calculated by dividing India's GLOBOCAN 2022 figures by the global GLOBOCAN 2022 totals from the two IARC fact sheets.

text.en: The latest GLOBOCAN edition estimates 79,360 new cervical cancer cases and 36,319 cervical cancer deaths in India in 2024; it remains the second most common cancer among Indian women (10.2% of their cancers).
text.hg: GLOBOCAN ke latest edition ke andaaze ke mutabik 2024 mein India mein cervical cancer ke 79,360 naye cases aaye aur isse 36,319 mautein hui; yeh ab bhi Indian mahilaon mein doosra sabse common cancer hai (unke kul cancer cases ka 10.2%).

facts.caveat: Not comparable with GLOBOCAN 2022 (1,27,526 cases, 79,906 deaths): the 2024 edition uses different registry inputs and methods, so the drop is mostly a change in estimation, not proof that cervical cancer fell by a third in two years. Say 'the latest estimate' rather than 'cases fell'.

text.en: The latest GLOBOCAN edition estimates 2,37,231 new breast cancer cases and 96,100 breast cancer deaths in India in 2024; breast cancer makes up 30.4% of all cancers in Indian women.
text.hg: GLOBOCAN ke latest edition ke andaaze ke mutabik 2024 mein India mein breast cancer ke 2,37,231 naye cases aaye aur isse 96,100 mautein hui; Indian mahilaon ke sabhi cancer cases mein 30.4% breast cancer ke hain.

facts.caveat: Not directly comparable with GLOBOCAN 2022 because methods and inputs changed. India's 2024 total: 15,62,581 new cancer cases and 9,01,828 cancer deaths.

text.en: Worldwide there were around 6,04,000 new cervical cancer cases and around 2,80,000 deaths in 2024, and women living with HIV are six times more likely to develop cervical cancer than women without HIV, according to WHO.
text.hg: WHO ke mutabik 2024 mein duniya bhar mein cervical cancer ke lagbhag 6,04,000 naye cases aaye aur lagbhag 2,80,000 mautein hui, aur HIV ke saath jee rahi mahilaon mein cervical cancer hone ka khatra bina HIV wali mahilaon ke muqable chhe guna zyada hota hai.

facts.caveat: Global figures from GLOBOCAN 2024 (IARC cervix fact sheet: 604,196 cases, 279,583 deaths); India's 2024 estimate is about 13% of both.

text.en: Under WHO's cervical cancer elimination strategy, launched on 17 November 2020 after the World Health Assembly resolution, 194 countries committed to reach by 2030: 90% of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15, 70% of women screened with a high-performance test by 35 and again by 45, and 90% of women with cervical disease treated.
text.hg: World Health Assembly ke resolution ke baad 17 November 2020 ko launch hui WHO ki cervical cancer elimination strategy ke tahat 194 deshon ne 2030 tak yeh targets poore karne ka commitment kiya: 15 saal ki umar tak 90% ladkiyon ka HPV ke khilaaf poora vaccination, 35 saal ki umar tak aur phir 45 tak 70% mahilaon ki high-performance test se screening, aur cervical disease wali 90% mahilaon ka ilaaj.

facts.value: 90-70-90 by 2030; elimination = 4 or fewer cases per 100,000 women
facts.caveat: The elimination threshold ('4 or fewer cases per 100 000 women') is from the WHO cervical cancer fact sheet (2026). WHO says full implementation could avert more than 40% of new cases and 5 million deaths by 2050.

text.en: Only 1.2% of Indian women aged 15-49 had ever been screened for cervical cancer in 2019-21, and just 0.6% had ever had a breast cancer screening test, against WHO's target of screening 70% of women.
text.hg: 2019-21 mein 15-49 saal ki Indian mahilaon mein se sirf 1.2% ki kabhi cervical cancer screening hui thi, aur sirf 0.6% ne kabhi breast cancer screening test karaya tha, jabki WHO ka target 70% mahilaon ki screening ka hai.

facts.value: Cervical 1.2%; breast 0.6%; oral 0.7% (women 15-49); cervical 2% among women 35-49
facts.caveat: Self-reported survey data from NFHS-5 (2019-21); WHO's 70% target applies to women aged 35 and 45. Coverage was highest in Tamil Nadu (7%), Puducherry (5%) and Mizoram (4%).

text.en: India launched a nationwide free HPV vaccination campaign on 28 February 2026 at Ajmer, Rajasthan, offering a single dose of Gardasil-4 to girls aged 14 at government health facilities, an annual cohort of about 1.2 crore girls.
text.hg: India ne 28 February 2026 ko Rajasthan ke Ajmer se HPV vaccination ka nationwide free campaign shuru kiya, jismein sarkari health facilities par 14 saal ki ladkiyon ko Gardasil-4 ki ek dose di jaati hai; har saal is umar ki lagbhag 1.2 crore ladkiyan hoti hain.

facts.value: Launched 28 Feb 2026; single-dose Gardasil-4; ~1.2 crore girls a year (PIB backgrounder: 1.15 crore)
facts.caveat: Vaccination is voluntary and needs parental consent recorded on U-WIN; a 90-day campaign was followed by routine immunisation-day availability. A same-day PIB backgrounder (PRID 2234009) gives the target as 1.15 crore girls; boys are not covered.

text.en: By 11 September 2026, more than 80 lakh (8 million) HPV vaccine doses had been given under India's national campaign, with Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Mizoram reporting 100% coverage of their identified target girls.
text.hg: 11 September 2026 tak India ke national campaign ke tahat HPV vaccine ki 80 lakh (8 million) se zyada doses di ja chuki thi, aur Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh aur Mizoram ne apni identified target ladkiyon mein 100% coverage report kiya.

facts.value: >80 lakh doses; UP >22 lakh girls; Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Assam >90%; Karnataka >85%
facts.caveat: 'Coverage' is against each state's identified target cohort, not the census cohort; 80 lakh doses is roughly two-thirds of the ~1.2 crore annual cohort, so lagging states pull the national figure down. No national coverage percentage was published.

text.en: The Union health ministry told Parliament on 21 July 2026 that 52,10,302 girls had received the HPV vaccine as of 15 July 2026, about 43% of the 1.2 crore target.
text.hg: Union health ministry ne 21 July 2026 ko Parliament ko bataya ki 15 July 2026 tak 52,10,302 ladkiyon ko HPV vaccine lag chuki thi, jo 1.2 crore ke target ka lagbhag 43% hai.

facts.caveat: Secondary report of a written answer by MoS Health Anupriya Patel; the 43% share is a calculation against the ~1.2 crore annual cohort. Check the Parliament answer before quoting precisely.

text.en: India's drugs regulator (DCGI) granted Serum Institute of India market authorisation for Cervavac, the first indigenously developed quadrivalent HPV vaccine against cervical cancer, on 12 July 2022.
text.hg: India ke drugs regulator (DCGI) ne 12 July 2022 ko Serum Institute of India ko Cervavac ke liye market authorisation di; yeh cervical cancer ke khilaaf desh mein hi develop hui pehli quadrivalent HPV vaccine hai.

facts.caveat: Cervavac was developed by Serum Institute of India with the Department of Biotechnology as a public-private partnership (The Tribune, 2022). The 2026 national programme uses Gardasil-4, not Cervavac.

text.en: Cervavac was unveiled on 1 September 2022 by Minister of State for Science and Technology Jitendra Singh, with Serum Institute saying it might cost Rs 200-400 a dose, two doses for ages 9-14 and three for ages 15-26.
text.hg: Cervavac ko 1 September 2022 ko Minister of State for Science and Technology Jitendra Singh ne pesh kiya; Serum Institute ne kaha ki iski keemat Rs 200-400 per dose ho sakti hai, 9-14 saal ki umar mein do doses aur 15-26 saal ki umar mein teen.

facts.value: Unveiled 1 Sept 2022; expected Rs 200-400 per dose
facts.caveat: Price was indicative at launch ('final prices will be fixed later'); actual market price not confirmed this session.

text.en: India's 2026 national HPV programme uses Gardasil-4, procured in partnership with GAVI, the Vaccine Alliance, rather than India's indigenously developed Cervavac.
text.hg: India ke 2026 ke national HPV programme mein desh mein hi develop hui Cervavac ki jagah Gardasil-4 use ho rahi hai, jise GAVI, the Vaccine Alliance ke saath partnership mein kharida gaya hai.

facts.caveat: The government has not publicly explained the choice in the sources reviewed; Cervavac is mentioned only in the list of previously received vaccines.

text.en: HPV types 16 and 18 account for more than 80% of cervical cancer cases in India, according to a Government of India (PIB) backgrounder.
text.hg: HPV types 16 and 18 account for more than 80% of cervical cancer cases in India, according to a Government of India (PIB) backgrounder.

facts.caveat: Government backgrounder citing a published study; Tribune (2022) quoted 83% of invasive cervical cancers.

text.en: 77.6% of Indian women aged 15-24 used a hygienic method of menstrual protection in 2019-21, yet nearly half (49.6%) still used cloth and only 64.4% used sanitary napkins.
text.hg: 2019-21 mein 15-24 saal ki 77.6% Indian mahilayein periods ke dauraan protection ka koi hygienic tareeka use karti thi, phir bhi lagbhag aadhi (49.6%) ab bhi kapda use karti thi aur sirf 64.4% sanitary napkins.

facts.value: 77.6% hygienic (NFHS-5, 2019-21); cloth 49.6%; sanitary napkins 64.4%; locally prepared napkins 15.0%
facts.caveat: NFHS counts locally prepared napkins, sanitary napkins, tampons and menstrual cups as hygienic; cloth is not, even though washed and dried cloth can be safe. Women may report more than one method, so percentages add up to more than 100.

text.en: In 2019-21, only 59.2% of young women in Bihar, 60.9% in Madhya Pradesh, 65.3% in Meghalaya, 66.9% in Gujarat and 67.0% in Assam used hygienic menstrual protection, compared with 99.1% in Puducherry and 98.4% in Tamil Nadu.
text.hg: 2019-21 mein Bihar ki sirf 59.2%, Madhya Pradesh ki 60.9%, Meghalaya ki 65.3%, Gujarat ki 66.9% aur Assam ki 67.0% young women periods mein hygienic protection use karti thi, jabki Puducherry mein yeh figure 99.1% aur Tamil Nadu mein 98.4% tha.

facts.value: Bihar 59.2%; MP 60.9%; Meghalaya 65.3%; Gujarat 66.9%; Assam 67.0%; Puducherry 99.1%; Tamil Nadu 98.4%
facts.caveat: Women aged 15-24 who have ever menstruated; survey data.

text.en: In 2019-21, 95.1% of young women in India's richest households used hygienic menstrual protection compared with 53.6% in the poorest, and 90.3% of those with 12 or more years of schooling compared with 43.5% of those with no schooling.
text.hg: 2019-21 mein India ke sabse ameer gharon ki 95.1% young women periods mein hygienic protection use karti thi, jabki sabse gareeb gharon mein yeh 53.6% tha; 12 ya usse zyada saal schooling wali mahilaon mein yeh 90.3% tha, jabki kabhi school na gayi mahilaon mein 43.5%.

facts.value: Richest 95.1% vs poorest 53.6%; 12+ years schooling 90.3% vs none 43.5%; urban 89.6% vs rural 72.6%; Scheduled Tribe 65.6%
facts.caveat: Women aged 15-24 who have ever menstruated.

text.en: On 30 January 2026, in Dr Jaya Thakur v. Government of India, the Supreme Court held that menstrual health is part of the right to life under Article 21 and directed that all schools provide functional gender-segregated toilets with water, free sanitary napkins and safe disposal systems.
text.hg: 30 January 2026 ko Dr Jaya Thakur v. Government of India case mein Supreme Court ne faisla diya ki menstrual health Article 21 ke tahat right to life ka hissa hai, aur nirdesh diya ki sabhi schools mein paani wale functional, gender-segregated toilets, free sanitary napkins aur safe disposal systems hon.

facts.value: Judgment of 30 Jan 2026, W.P.(C) No. 1000/2022, 2026 LiveLaw (SC) 94; Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan
facts.caveat: The court also ordered 'MHM corners' with spare uniforms, NCERT/SCERT gender-responsive curricula, sensitisation of boys and male teachers, and District Education Officer inspections. On 1 Sept 2026 it changed the pad standard from oxo-biodegradable to biodegradable/compostable (ISO 17088 with IS 5405).

text.en: At a 1 September 2026 hearing, the Supreme Court said it was discontented with states' compliance on menstrual hygiene in schools; the Centre's affidavit showed 39,439 girls' toilets had been identified as needing to be made functional, of which 30,458 were built, 4,236 under construction and 4,745 still a gap.
text.hg: 1 September 2026 ki hearing mein Supreme Court ne kaha ki woh schools mein menstrual hygiene par states ke compliance se naakhush hai; Centre ke affidavit ke mutabik ladkiyon ke 39,439 toilets aise identify kiye gaye the jinhe functional banana zaroori tha, jinmein se 30,458 ban chuke the, 4,236 ban rahe the aur 4,745 ki kami ab bhi baaki thi.

facts.caveat: Toilet counts come from the Union government's affidavit of 31 August 2026, quoted in the order; the gap was identified from UDISE+ 2024-25 and states had been asked to close it before 8 March 2026. The court flagged data discrepancies in states including Tamil Nadu, Assam, Karnataka, Bihar, Gujarat, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh, and found Punjab's report illegible.

text.en: In an order reported on 15 October 2026, the Supreme Court gave states 'one last opportunity' to report compliance with its menstrual hygiene directions, warning that it would issue contempt notices to the Chief Secretaries of states that failed to respond; the case is listed next on 14 December 2026.
text.hg: In an order reported on 15 October 2026, the Supreme Court gave states 'one last opportunity' to report compliance with its menstrual hygiene directions, warning that it would issue contempt notices to the Chief Secretaries of states that failed to respond; the case is listed next on 14 December 2026.

facts.caveat: The exact hearing date was not confirmed: the 1 September 2026 order listed the case for 29 September 2026, and LiveLaw's 15 October 2026 report describes the order only as recent. The Union's lawyer told the Court that states had not responded to the Centre's requests for information.

text.en: In December 2024 the Union government told the Supreme Court that a national menstrual hygiene policy for school-going girls had recently been framed and would have to be implemented by states, with distribution mainly through schools and anganwadis.
text.hg: December 2024 mein Union government ne Supreme Court ko bataya ki school jaane wali ladkiyon ke liye ek national menstrual hygiene policy haal hi mein banayi gayi hai, jise states ko laagu karna hoga, aur distribution mainly schools aur anganwadis ke zariye hoga.

facts.value: National policy framed (late 2024); judgment reserved 10 Dec 2024
facts.caveat: The petition, filed in 2022, sought free sanitary napkins and separate toilets for adolescent girls in schools.

text.en: An ICMR-funded national study of women aged 18-40 found PCOS prevalence of 7.2% by the strict NIH criteria, 13.6% by AE-PCOS criteria and 19.6% by the broader Rotterdam criteria, meaning up to 1 in 5 Indian women of reproductive age may have the condition.
text.hg: ICMR-funded ek national study mein 18-40 saal ki mahilaon mein PCOS prevalence strict NIH criteria se 7.2%, AE-PCOS criteria se 13.6% aur broader Rotterdam criteria se 19.6% mili; iska matlab hai ki reproductive age ki 5 mein se 1 tak Indian mahilaon ko yeh condition ho sakti hai.

facts.caveat: Ganie MA et al., JAMA Network Open, 23 Oct 2024; community sample of women aged 18-40 across five zones and 8 states (9,824 recruited per Key Points; 8,993 enrolled per abstract). Prevalence depends heavily on the diagnostic criteria used.

text.en: Among Indian women with PCOS in the ICMR national study, 43.2% had obesity, 91.9% had abnormal blood lipids, 32.9% had fatty liver disease and 24.9% had metabolic syndrome.
text.hg: ICMR ki national study mein PCOS wali Indian mahilaon mein se 43.2% ko obesity thi, 91.9% ke blood lipids abnormal the, 32.9% ko fatty liver disease thi aur 24.9% ko metabolic syndrome tha.

facts.value: Obesity 43.2%; dyslipidaemia 91.9%; NAFLD 32.9%; metabolic syndrome 24.9%; hypertension 8.3%; diabetes 3.3-3.4%
facts.caveat: Comorbidity rates are among women with PCOS in the study sample.

text.en: WHO estimates that PCOS affects 10-13% of women of reproductive age worldwide and that up to 70% of women with PCOS do not know they have it.
text.hg: WHO ka andaaza hai ki duniya bhar mein reproductive age ki 10-13% mahilaon ko PCOS hai, aur PCOS wali 70% tak mahilaon ko pata hi nahi hota ki unhe yeh hai.

facts.caveat: WHO fact sheet dated 22 January 2026; WHO calls PCOS the most common cause of anovulation and a leading cause of infertility.

text.en: Endometriosis affects an estimated 10% of women of reproductive age worldwide, about 190 million women, and diagnosis takes on average 4 to 12 years, according to WHO.
text.hg: WHO ke mutabik duniya bhar mein reproductive age ki andaazan 10% mahilaon, yaani lagbhag 190 million mahilaon ko endometriosis hai, aur iska diagnosis hone mein average 4 se 12 saal lagte hain.

facts.caveat: WHO fact sheet dated 15 October 2025. No reliable India-specific prevalence estimate was confirmed; do not apply 10% to India's population as if measured.

text.en: About 17.5% of adults worldwide, roughly 1 in 6 people, experience infertility in their lifetime, according to a WHO report released on 4 April 2023, with similar rates in rich (17.8%) and poorer (16.5%) countries.
text.hg: 4 April 2023 ko jaari WHO ki ek report ke mutabik duniya bhar mein lagbhag 17.5% adults, yaani mote taur par har 6 mein se 1 insaan, zindagi mein kabhi na kabhi infertility face karte hain; ameer (17.8%) aur gareeb (16.5%) deshon mein yeh dar lagbhag ek jaisi hai.

facts.caveat: Based on studies from 1990 to 2021; infertility defined as no pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected sex. WHO notes treatment is largely paid out of pocket. Not an India-specific estimate.

text.en: Section 3 of India's Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 bans advertising any drug for 'the procurement of miscarriage in women or prevention of conception in women', 'the maintenance or improvement of the capacity of human beings for sexual pleasure' or 'the correction of menstrual disorder in women', or for diagnosing, curing or preventing diseases listed in the Act's Schedule, which include venereal diseases.
text.hg: Section 3 of India's Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 bans advertising any drug for 'the procurement of miscarriage in women or prevention of conception in women', 'the maintenance or improvement of the capacity of human beings for sexual pleasure' or 'the correction of menstrual disorder in women', or for diagnosing, curing or preventing diseases listed in the Act's Schedule, which include venereal diseases.

facts.caveat: Section 3 text as quoted in the Supreme Court's order of 26 March 2025; LiveLaw's report of that order says the Schedule includes venereal diseases, cancer, diabetes and others. Section 5 extends the ban to 'magic remedies' (talismans, mantras, amulets) claimed to work for the same purposes.

text.en: Under the 1954 Drugs and Magic Remedies Act, advertising drugs that claim to treat conditions listed in the Act's Schedule, such as sexual impotence and venereal diseases including syphilis and gonorrhoea, is a crime: a first conviction carries up to six months in jail, a fine, or both, and a repeat conviction up to one year, a fine, or both.
text.hg: Under the 1954 Drugs and Magic Remedies Act, advertising drugs that claim to treat conditions listed in the Act's Schedule, such as sexual impotence and venereal diseases including syphilis and gonorrhoea, is a crime: a first conviction carries up to six months in jail, a fine, or both, and a repeat conviction up to one year, a fine, or both.

facts.value: First conviction: up to 6 months, fine, or both; subsequent: up to 1 year, fine, or both (Section 7); cognizable (Section 9A)
facts.caveat: The Schedule (added by a 1963 amendment) lists 54 diseases and conditions according to Wikipedia; the official India Code text could not be accessed, so only the entries named here were cross-checked (impotence: LiveLaw 2019; venereal diseases: LiveLaw 2025 and the 1954 text). Because the offence is cognizable, police must register an FIR on a complaint.

text.en: On 26 March 2025, in Indian Medical Association v. Union of India, the Supreme Court said that although the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act was more than 70 years old, 'there is no implementation of the 1954 Act in its true letter and spirit', and ordered states to appoint enforcement officers within one month and to set up public complaint mechanisms, such as a toll-free number or email, within two months.
text.hg: On 26 March 2025, in Indian Medical Association v. Union of India, the Supreme Court said that although the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act was more than 70 years old, 'there is no implementation of the 1954 Act in its true letter and spirit', and ordered states to appoint enforcement officers within one month and to set up public complaint mechanisms, such as a toll-free number or email, within two months.

facts.value: Officers within 1 month; grievance mechanism within 2 months; W.P.(C) 645/2022
facts.caveat: Bench of Justices Abhay S. Oka and Ujjal Bhuyan. The case began as an Indian Medical Association petition about misleading health advertisements; the amicus told the court that many states only issued warnings instead of prosecuting. States and the Union were to report compliance by the end of June 2025.

text.en: In 2015-16 only 57.6% of Indian women aged 15-24 used a hygienic method of menstrual protection; 62% used cloth and 42% used sanitary napkins.
text.hg: 2015-16 mein 15-24 saal ki sirf 57.6% Indian mahilayein periods ke dauraan protection ka koi hygienic tareeka use karti thi; 62% kapda use karti thi aur 42% sanitary napkins.

facts.caveat: NFHS-4 did not count menstrual cups as hygienic (NFHS-5 did), a minor definitional difference. Rural 48% vs urban 78%.

text.en: In the latest GLOBOCAN estimates for 2024, India accounted for about 13% of the world's new cervical cancer cases (79,360 of 6,04,196) and about 13% of cervical cancer deaths (36,319 of 2,79,583).
text.hg: 2024 ke liye GLOBOCAN ke latest estimates mein duniya bhar ke cervical cancer ke naye cases mein se lagbhag 13% (6,04,196 mein se 79,360) aur isse hui mauton mein se lagbhag 13% (2,79,583 mein se 36,319) India mein the.

facts.caveat: Calculated from the two IARC GLOBOCAN 2024 fact sheets. The share is far lower than in GLOBOCAN 2022 (about 19% of cases, 23% of deaths) because India's estimate was revised sharply downward between editions; treat the change as methodological, not as a real two-year fall.

text.en: India's National AIDS and STD Control Programme Phase V, run as a fully funded central scheme from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026, aimed to cut annual new HIV infections and AIDS-related deaths by 80% from 2010 levels.
text.hg: India ka National AIDS and STD Control Programme Phase V 1 April 2021 se 31 March 2026 tak ek fully funded central scheme ke roop mein chala; iska goal saalana naye HIV infections aur AIDS se judi mauton ko 2010 ke level se 80% kam karna tha.

facts.value: 80% reduction target vs 2010; outlay Rs 15,471.94 crore
facts.caveat: Outlay of Rs 15,471.94 crore is from the PIB World AIDS Day backgrounder (30 Nov 2025). By 2024 deaths were down 81.4% (target met) but new infections only 48.7% (target missed).

text.en: In 2010 India had an estimated 1.25 lakh new HIV infections and 1.73 lakh AIDS-related deaths, with adult HIV prevalence of 0.33%.
text.hg: 2010 mein India mein andaazan 1.25 lakh naye HIV infections hue aur AIDS se judi 1.73 lakh mautein hui, aur adults mein HIV prevalence 0.33% thi.

facts.value: 1.25 lakh new infections; 1.73 lakh deaths; 0.33% prevalence (2010)
facts.caveat: Back-calculated 2010 values from the latest (2025) estimation round; older reports give different 2010 numbers.

text.en: NACO estimates that the number of people living with HIV in India fell from about 32 lakh in 2005 to about 27 lakh in 2010, and has since stayed at roughly 25-26 lakh (25.61 lakh in 2024).
text.hg: NACO estimates that the number of people living with HIV in India fell from about 32 lakh in 2005 to about 27 lakh in 2010, and has since stayed at roughly 25-26 lakh (25.61 lakh in 2024).

facts.caveat: Modelled back-series. Do not print a precise peak: the 2025 report says 39 lakh in its text, its chart shows about 36 lakh around 1999-2000, and the 2024 report said about 37 lakh.

text.en: India's AIDS programme carried out 4.13 crore HIV tests among at-risk clients in 2024-25 with 0.40% testing positive; people who walked in on their own made up only 14% of tests but had the highest positivity, 1.1%.
text.hg: 2024-25 mein India ke AIDS programme ne at-risk clients ke 4.13 crore HIV tests kiye, jinmein se 0.40% positive nikle; khud chal kar test karwane aaye logon ke tests kul ka sirf 14% the, lekin unmein positivity sabse zyada, 1.1%, thi.

facts.value: 4.13 crore tests; 0.40% positivity; walk-ins 14% of tests, 1.1% positivity
facts.caveat: Counts tests, not people; excludes testing of pregnant women reported separately.

text.en: On World AIDS Day 2025 the Union health minister said 85% of people living with HIV in India knew their status and treatment coverage stood at 88%, slightly higher than the 83.9% and 86.6% reported in NACO's own 2025 Sankalak report.
text.hg: World AIDS Day 2025 par Union health minister ne kaha ki India mein HIV ke saath jee rahe 85% logon ko apna status pata hai aur treatment coverage 88% hai; yeh figures NACO ki apni 2025 ki Sankalak report mein diye gaye 83.9% aur 86.6% se thode zyada hain.

facts.caveat: The minister's figures may refer to a different reference period; for print, prefer the Sankalak 2024-25 cascade (83.9-86.6-97.6). The article's current headline gives a 49% fall in new infections and 81% fall in AIDS deaths between 2010 and 2024, matching NACO; only its URL still carries an earlier '32% ... 69%' headline, which should not be used.

text.en: India's HPV vaccine is offered free only at government facilities, from Ayushman Arogya Mandir primary health centres to medical colleges, in all 36 States and UTs; vaccination is voluntary and parental consent is mandatory.
text.hg: India mein HPV vaccine sabhi 36 States aur UTs mein sirf sarkari facilities par free di jaati hai, Ayushman Arogya Mandir primary health centres se lekar medical colleges tak; vaccination voluntary hai aur parents ki consent zaroori hai.

facts.value: Free; voluntary; parental consent mandatory; 36 States/UTs
facts.caveat: Girls who were already vaccinated privately (Gardasil, Gardasil-9, Cervarix or Cervavac) are recorded on U-WIN rather than re-vaccinated.

text.en: In 2024-25, shared needles and syringes were the most commonly reported route of infection among people newly diagnosed with HIV in Arunachal Pradesh (72%), Tripura (67%), Assam (60%) and Punjab (56%), against 11.5% nationally; in Assam the share was just 2.1% in 2017-18.
text.hg: In 2024-25, shared needles and syringes were the most commonly reported route of infection among people newly diagnosed with HIV in Arunachal Pradesh (72%), Tripura (67%), Assam (60%) and Punjab (56%), against 11.5% nationally; in Assam the share was just 2.1% in 2017-18.

facts.value: Arunachal Pradesh 71.7%; Tripura 66.8%; Assam 59.7%; Punjab 56.2%; India 11.5% (2024-25); Assam 2.1% (2017-18)
facts.caveat: Self-reported route among people newly diagnosed through NACO services. Punjab's share applies to 11,520 new diagnoses (the fifth-highest of any state), or roughly 6,500 people in one year.

text.en: In 2024-25, 6.6 lakh spouses, partners and children of people living with HIV were tested through NACO's index testing (partner notification) service, and 4.1% tested positive, about ten times the 0.40% positivity among all at-risk people tested that year.
text.hg: In 2024-25, 6.6 lakh spouses, partners and children of people living with HIV were tested through NACO's index testing (partner notification) service, and 4.1% tested positive, about ten times the 0.40% positivity among all at-risk people tested that year.

facts.value: 6.6 lakh contacts tested; 4.1% positive (12.1 lakh PLHIV offered, 10.8 lakh accepted)
facts.caveat: Index testing is voluntary and done with the consent of the person living with HIV; contacts include sexual partners, needle-sharing partners and biological children under 19.

text.en: Of the 17.54 lakh people on antiretroviral therapy at India's government ART centres in March 2025, about 8.67 lakh were men, 7.98 lakh women, 7,000 hijra/transgender people and around 80,000 children.
text.hg: Of the 17.54 lakh people on antiretroviral therapy at India's government ART centres in March 2025, about 8.67 lakh were men, 7.98 lakh women, 7,000 hijra/transgender people and around 80,000 children.

facts.value: Men 8.67 lakh; women 7.98 lakh; H/TG 7,000; children ~80,000 (March 2025)
facts.caveat: Covers only people on treatment in the government programme; about 1.06 lakh more are estimated to be on ART in the private sector.

text.en: India's national toll-free AIDS helpline, 1097, received 4,32,474 calls in 2024-25 and offers confidential counselling round the clock in 16 languages.
text.hg: India's national toll-free AIDS helpline, 1097, received 4,32,474 calls in 2024-25 and offers confidential counselling round the clock in 16 languages.

facts.caveat: Call volume jumped from 37,891 in November to 97,484 in December 2024 after SMS promotion campaigns, so annual totals swing with publicity.

title.en: Gender, LGBTQ+ rights and mental health
title.hg: Gender, LGBTQ+ rights aur mental health

text.en: Census 2011 counted 4,87,803 people in India in the "other" gender category, the figure the government still uses as the transgender population.
text.hg: Census 2011 mein India mein 4,87,803 logon ko "other" gender category mein gina gaya tha; sarkar aaj bhi isi figure ko transgender population maanti hai.

facts.caveat: Census 2011 did not specifically enumerate transgender persons and many recorded themselves as male or female, so this is widely seen as an undercount. The exact figure 4,87,803 is also quoted (from a PIB release of 25 June 2019) in the 2026 Kalki Subramaniam petition. PIB also notes that the 'other' category includes anyone who chose to record 'other', not only transgender persons.

text.en: On 15 April 2014, in NALSA v. Union of India (Writ Petition (Civil) No. 400 of 2012), the Supreme Court recognised transgender persons as a "third gender", upheld their right to self-identify their gender and extended them protection under Articles 14, 15, 16, 19 and 21.
text.hg: 15 April 2014 ko NALSA v. Union of India (Writ Petition (Civil) No. 400 of 2012) mein Supreme Court ne transgender logon ko "third gender" ke roop mein recognise kiya, apna gender khud identify karne ke unke right ko uphold kiya, aur unhe Articles 14, 15, 16, 19 aur 21 ke tahat protection di.

facts.caveat: Reported as (2014) 5 SCC 438; bench of Justices K.S. Radhakrishnan and A.K. Sikri.

text.en: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 came into force on 10 January 2020, its Rules were notified on 25 September 2020, and the National Portal for Transgender Persons, which issues transgender certificates and identity cards online, was launched on 25 November 2020.
text.hg: 10 January 2020 ko Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 laagu hua, 25 September 2020 ko iske Rules notify kiye gaye, aur 25 November 2020 ko National Portal for Transgender Persons launch hua, jo online transgender certificate aur identity card issue karta hai.

facts.caveat: The Kalki petition and PIB's 2025 backgrounder give 25 September 2020 for the Rules; a June 2022 PIB explainer gives 29 September 2020 as the date they were published in the Gazette.

text.en: Section 4(2) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 gave every person recognised as transgender "a right to self-perceived gender identity".
text.hg: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 ke Section 4(2) ne transgender ke roop mein recognised har vyakti ko "a right to self-perceived gender identity" diya, yaani khud mehsoos ki gayi gender identity ka right.

facts.caveat: Checked against the Gazette text of the Act (PRS copy). Sub-section omitted by Section 3 of the 2026 Amendment Act, in force from 25 May 2026 (see gen-tg-amendment-2026-medical-board).

text.en: By December 2024, the National Portal for Transgender Persons had issued 24,015 transgender certificates, equal to about 5% of the 4.87 lakh people counted in the "other" gender category in Census 2011.
text.hg: December 2024 tak National Portal for Transgender Persons ne 24,015 transgender certificates issue kiye the, jo Census 2011 mein "other" gender category mein gine gaye 4.87 lakh logon ke lagbhag 5% ke barabar hai.

facts.caveat: Annexure to a Parliament reply released by PIB in December 2024. The 5% share is a calculation against the Census 2011 count, which is itself an undercount.

text.en: A writ petition filed in the Supreme Court on 15 June 2026 cited Ministry of Social Justice data released in June 2026 showing that only 33,189 transgender certificates had been issued nationwide through the National Portal, about 7% of the Census 2011 count.
text.hg: 15 June 2026 ko Supreme Court mein file hui ek writ petition mein June 2026 mein jaari Ministry of Social Justice ke data ka hawala diya gaya, jiske mutabik National Portal ke zariye poore desh mein sirf 33,189 transgender certificates issue hue the, yaani Census 2011 ki ginti ka lagbhag 7%.

facts.caveat: Figure as quoted in a petitioner's filing (Annexure P-11, PIB release dated 11.06.2026); the original PIB release was not located in this session. The 7% share is a calculation.

text.en: As of November 2025, India had 21 Garima Greh shelter homes for destitute transgender persons, spread across 17 states, under the SMILE scheme launched on 12 February 2022.
text.hg: November 2025 tak, 12 February 2022 ko launch hui SMILE scheme ke tahat, India mein besahara transgender logon ke liye 21 Garima Greh shelter homes the, jo 17 states mein faile hue the.

facts.caveat: Three more Garima Grehs had been sanctioned (Puducherry, Basti, Gautambudhnagar).

text.en: As of November 2025, only 20 states and union territories had set up Transgender Protection Cells and 25 had set up Transgender Welfare Boards, five years after the 2020 Rules required every state to set up a protection cell.
text.hg: November 2025 tak sirf 20 states aur union territories ne Transgender Protection Cells aur 25 ne Transgender Welfare Boards banaye the, jabki 2020 ke Rules ne paanch saal pehle hi har state ke liye protection cell banana zaroori kar diya tha.

facts.caveat: India has 36 states and union territories.

text.en: Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026 within 12 days of its introduction: it was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 13 March 2026, passed by the Lok Sabha on 24 March 2026 and by the Rajya Sabha on 25 March 2026.
text.hg: Parliament ne Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026 ko introduce hone ke 12 dinon ke andar pass kar diya: ise 13 March 2026 ko Lok Sabha mein introduce kiya gaya, 24 March 2026 ko Lok Sabha ne aur 25 March 2026 ko Rajya Sabha ne ise pass kiya.

facts.caveat: Bill of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.

text.en: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026 (Act No. 3 of 2026) received Presidential assent on 30 March 2026 and was brought into force from 25 May 2026 by a government notification.
text.hg: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026 (Act No. 3 of 2026) received Presidential assent on 30 March 2026 and was brought into force from 25 May 2026 by a government notification.

facts.caveat: Commencement as cited in a Supreme Court petition (notification S.O. 2620(E) of 22 May 2026, Annexure P-15 of the Kalki Subramaniam petition); the notification itself was not opened.

text.en: The 2026 amendment deletes the right to self-perceived gender identity (Section 4(2)) and makes a District Magistrate issue a transgender certificate only after examining the recommendation of a medical board headed by a Chief Medical Officer or Deputy Chief Medical Officer.
text.hg: 2026 ka amendment self-perceived gender identity ke right (Section 4(2)) ko hata deta hai, aur tay karta hai ki District Magistrate transgender certificate tabhi issue karenge jab woh ek aise medical board ki recommendation examine kar lein jiske head Chief Medical Officer ya Deputy Chief Medical Officer hon.

facts.caveat: This reverses the self-identification principle of NALSA (2014). The amendment is under challenge in the Supreme Court.

text.en: The 2026 amendment redefines a transgender person to mean people with socio-cultural identities such as kinner, hijra, aravani and jogta, eunuchs, intersex persons, and people forced into a transgender identity, and states that the term does not include "persons with different sexual orientations and self-perceived sexual identities".
text.hg: 2026 ka amendment transgender person ki definition badalta hai: ab iska matlab kinner, hijra, aravani aur jogta jaisi socio-cultural identities wale log, eunuchs, intersex persons, aur zabardasti transgender identity apnane par majboor kiye gaye log hain; amendment yeh bhi kehta hai ki is term mein "persons with different sexual orientations and self-perceived sexual identities" shaamil nahi hain.

facts.caveat: PRS Legislative Research's bill summary notes that trans-men, trans-women and genderqueer persons, named in the 2019 definition, are dropped.

text.en: Under the 2026 amendment, kidnapping an adult and causing grievous hurt to force them to assume a transgender identity is punishable with rigorous imprisonment of 10 years to life and a fine of at least Rs 2 lakh; for a child victim it is life imprisonment and a fine of at least Rs 5 lakh.
text.hg: 2026 ke amendment ke tahat, kisi adult ko kidnap karke aur use grievous hurt (gambhir chot) pahunchakar transgender identity apnane par majboor karne ki saza 10 saal se lekar umrqaid tak ki rigorous imprisonment aur kam se kam Rs 2 lakh ka fine hai; agar victim bachcha ho, to saza umrqaid aur kam se kam Rs 5 lakh ka fine hai.

facts.caveat: New Section 18(e) and 18(f), substituted by Section 7 of the Amendment Act.

text.en: Sexual abuse of a transgender person in India is punishable with only six months to two years in prison and a fine under Section 18(d) of the Transgender Persons Act, a range the 2026 amendment left unchanged.
text.hg: India mein kisi transgender vyakti ke sexual abuse ki saza Transgender Persons Act ke Section 18(d) ke tahat sirf chhah mahine se do saal tak ki jail aur fine hai, aur 2026 ke amendment ne is range mein koi badlav nahi kiya.

facts.caveat: Same range as the original 2019 Section 18(d). Rape under Section 63 of the BNS covers only women as victims (see gen-bns-s63-man-woman).

text.en: On 17 August 2026, a Supreme Court bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant heard challenges to the 2026 transgender amendment, and the Union told the court that identity cards already issued under the 2019 Act would continue to operate while the case is pending.
text.hg: 17 August 2026 ko Chief Justice Surya Kant ki aguwai wali Supreme Court bench ne 2026 ke transgender amendment ke khilaf challenges par sunwai ki, aur Union (Centre) ne court ko bataya ki case pending rehne tak 2019 Act ke tahat pehle se issue hue identity cards chalte rahenge.

facts.caveat: Petitions include those of Akkai Padmashali and Kalki Subramaniam (W.P.(C) 548/2026 and connected matters); the court asked the Union to file a reply and listed the matter after four weeks. No later hearing report was found on SCO's case page as of November 2026.

text.en: On 6 September 2018, a five-judge Supreme Court bench in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India unanimously read down Section 377 of the IPC, decriminalising consensual sex between adults of the same sex while keeping non-consensual acts and bestiality as crimes.
text.hg: 6 September 2018 ko Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India mein Supreme Court ki paanch judges ki bench ne unanimously IPC ke Section 377 ko read down kiya, jisse same-sex adults ke beech consent se bane sexual relations crime nahi rahe, jabki bina consent ke acts aur bestiality (jaanvaron ke saath sexual acts) crime bane rahe.

facts.caveat: Bench: CJI Dipak Misra and Justices R.F. Nariman, A.M. Khanwilkar, D.Y. Chandrachud and Indu Malhotra. Reported as (2018) 10 SCC 1.

text.en: The Delhi High Court decriminalised consensual gay sex on 2 July 2009 in Naz Foundation, but the Supreme Court reversed that verdict on 11 December 2013 in Suresh Kumar Koushal, recriminalising it for nearly five years until Navtej Singh Johar in September 2018.
text.hg: The Delhi High Court decriminalised consensual gay sex on 2 July 2009 in Naz Foundation, but the Supreme Court reversed that verdict on 11 December 2013 in Suresh Kumar Koushal, recriminalising it for nearly five years until Navtej Singh Johar in September 2018.

facts.caveat: Koushal: Civil Appeal No. 10972 of 2013, reported as (2014) 1 SCC 1; judgment written by Justice G.S. Singhvi.

text.en: On 17 October 2023, a five-judge Supreme Court bench in Supriyo v. Union of India unanimously held that there is no fundamental right to marry and declined to recognise same-sex marriage, leaving it to Parliament.
text.hg: 17 October 2023 ko Supriyo v. Union of India mein Supreme Court ki paanch judges ki bench ne unanimously kaha ki shaadi ka koi fundamental right nahi hai, aur same-sex marriage ko recognise karne se inkaar karte hue yeh maamla Parliament par chhod diya.

facts.caveat: Citation 2023 INSC 920; W.P. (C) 1011/2022. Bench: CJI D.Y. Chandrachud and Justices S.K. Kaul, S.R. Bhat, Hima Kohli and P.S. Narasimha.

text.en: In the 2023 Supriyo judgment, the Supreme Court split 3:2 against a right of queer couples to enter civil unions: Chief Justice Chandrachud and Justice Kaul would have recognised it, while Justices Bhat, Kohli and Narasimha held no such right exists.
text.hg: 2023 ke Supriyo judgment mein Supreme Court ne 3:2 ke split faisle se queer couples ke civil union mein aane ke right ke khilaf raay di: Chief Justice Chandrachud aur Justice Kaul is right ko recognise karne ke paksh mein the, jabki Justices Bhat, Kohli aur Narasimha ne kaha ki aisa koi right exist nahi karta.

facts.caveat: The majority also read the adoption law as covering joint adoption by married couples, which excludes queer couples (3:2).

text.en: The Supreme Court held in October 2023 that a transgender person in a heterosexual relationship is entitled to marry under existing marriage laws.
text.hg: Supreme Court ne October 2023 mein kaha ki heterosexual relationship mein rehne wale transgender vyakti ko maujooda marriage laws ke tahat shaadi karne ka haq hai.

facts.caveat: Held by CJI Chandrachud with Justice Bhat concurring.

text.en: On 9 January 2025, the Supreme Court dismissed the review petitions against its October 2023 same-sex marriage judgment, finding no error apparent in it.
text.hg: 9 January 2025 ko Supreme Court ne apne October 2023 ke same-sex marriage judgment ke khilaf review petitions dismiss kar di, kyunki use judgment mein koi saaf dikhne wali galti (error apparent) nahi mili.

facts.caveat: Five-judge review bench headed by Justice B.R. Gavai (The Hindu, 9 January 2025).

text.en: On 16 April 2024, following the Supriyo judgment, the Centre set up a six-member committee chaired by the Cabinet Secretary to recommend measures against discrimination, violence and involuntary medical treatment of queer persons.
text.hg: Supriyo judgment ke baad, 16 April 2024 ko Centre ne Cabinet Secretary ki chairmanship mein chhah members ki ek committee banayi, taaki woh queer logon ke saath discrimination, violence aur unki marzi ke bina hone wale medical treatment ke khilaf measures suggest kare.

facts.caveat: Members: Secretaries of Home, Women and Child Development, Health, Legislative Department, and Social Justice (convener). Its terms of reference do not mention legal recognition of couples. No report from it was found in this session.

text.en: In June 2021, the Madras High Court (Justice N. Anand Venkatesh) in S. Sushma v. Commissioner of Police directed that any attempt to medically "cure" or change the sexual orientation or gender identity of LGBTQIA+ people be prohibited, with action including withdrawal of the licence of professionals involved.
text.hg: June 2021 mein Madras High Court (Justice N. Anand Venkatesh) ne S. Sushma v. Commissioner of Police mein direct kiya ki LGBTQIA+ logon ki sexual orientation ya gender identity ko medically "cure" karne ya badalne ki kisi bhi koshish par rok lagayi jaye, aur ismein shaamil professionals ke khilaf action ho, jismein unka licence wapas lena bhi shaamil hai.

facts.caveat: Writ Petition No. 7284 of 2021, filed by a lesbian couple; order dated 7 June 2021. The ruling also ordered sensitisation of police, judiciary, schools and health workers, and the court kept the case pending to monitor compliance.

text.en: In a letter dated 25 August 2022 to all state medical councils, the National Medical Commission declared that conducting "conversion therapy" on LGBTQIA+ persons is professional misconduct, after the Madras High Court directed it to do so.
text.hg: National Medical Commission (NMC) ne sabhi state medical councils ko bheje 25 August 2022 ke letter mein declare kiya ki LGBTQIA+ logon par "conversion therapy" karna professional misconduct hai; usne yeh kadam Madras High Court ke direction ke baad uthaya.

facts.caveat: Issued by the NMC's Ethics and Medical Registration Board in compliance with the Madras High Court's order of 8 July 2022; it makes conversion therapy professional misconduct under the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations, 2002, so it binds registered medical practitioners. The court's direction refers to attempts to 'medically cure' sexual orientation or gender identity.

text.en: Section 21 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 bars discrimination in mental health care on any basis, naming gender, sex and sexual orientation among the protected grounds.
text.hg: Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 ka Section 21 mental health care mein kisi bhi aadhaar par discrimination par rok lagata hai, aur protected grounds mein gender, sex aur sexual orientation ka naam lekar zikr karta hai.

facts.caveat: Checked against the Gazette text of the Act (PRS copy). The section applies to health care for persons with mental illness.

text.en: Section 63 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 defines rape as an act committed by "a man" against "a woman", so an adult man cannot legally be a victim of rape in India.
text.hg: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 ka Section 63 rape ko "a man" (ek aadmi) dwara "a woman" (ek aurat) ke khilaf kiya gaya act define karta hai, isliye India mein kanooni taur par koi adult aadmi rape ka victim nahi ho sakta.

facts.caveat: Same structure as Section 375 IPC. Child victims of any sex are covered by the POCSO Act, 2012. Checked against the official Gazette text of the BNS.

text.en: When the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code on 1 July 2024, it dropped Section 377, which had punished non-consensual "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" with any man, woman or animal with up to life imprisonment, and added no replacement.
text.hg: Jab 1 July 2024 ko Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) ne Indian Penal Code (IPC) ki jagah li, to usne Section 377 hata diya aur uski jagah kuch nahi joda; yeh section kisi bhi aadmi, aurat ya jaanvar ke saath bina consent ke "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" ke liye umrqaid tak ki saza deta tha.

facts.caveat: Scroll report dated 29 August 2024. Petitioners argue that an FIR for rape of a man cannot be registered under the BNS; police may use lesser offences such as hurt.

text.en: On 10 November 2023, Parliament's Standing Committee on Home Affairs warned that omitting Section 377 would leave non-consensual sexual offences against men, transgender persons and animals unpunished, and recommended keeping it; the government did not accept the recommendation.
